title: Namespaces and usings
hook: Namespaces are the hierarchical names of types, not folders. `using` is an import alias for that hierarchy. File-scoped namespaces and `global using` cut ceremony without changing the CLR type name.

sections.heading: Namespaces, using, file-scoped, global using
sections.prose: A type’s identity is `Namespace.TypeName` (plus assembly). Folders are a convention; the compiler does not infer a namespace from disk. `using Acme.Messaging;` lets you write `SqsEnvelope` instead of `Acme.Messaging.SqsEnvelope`. File-scoped form `namespace Acme.Messaging;` applies to the whole file and avoids an extra brace layer — default in current templates. `global using Acme.Messaging;` (often in `GlobalUsings.cs` or generated by implicit usings) applies to every file in the compilation. `using static System.Math;` imports members. `using Json = System.Text.Json;` is an alias. None of this is Node’s `import { x } from 'pkg'` — you still need a project reference or NuGet package; `using` never downloads code.

snippets.label: File-scoped namespace vs fully qualified name
snippets.explanation: Interviewers sometimes ask if moving a file changes its type name. Only a namespace declaration (or implicit file-scoped default in some SDK generators) does.

interviewTakeaways: `using` is compile-time name resolution; the assembly reference is a separate project concern.
File-scoped namespaces are equivalent to a block namespace wrapping the file.
`global using` is compilation-wide; overuse hides where a type actually lives.
commonPitfalls: Assuming the folder path is the namespace (Java package muscle memory).
Adding `using` without a package reference and wondering why restore did nothing.
Two `global using` aliases that collide after a SDK bump of implicit usings.

jsTsCorrelations.note: `import` both names and loads a module. C# `using` only shortens names; loading is assembly references.
TS `namespace` is mostly legacy; ESM is the unit. C# namespaces remain the primary grouping for types inside assemblies.
